Neonatal Sandwich terns (Thalasseus sandvicensis) emerge from eggs incubated for a period of approximately 22 days [ab = approximately 22 days] under stable thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that falls within the typical range for medium-sized terns and reflects the efficient heat transfer provided by attentive biparental incubation. The newly hatched chicks are remarkably small, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 28 grams [Wwb = 28 grams], a value that underscores their altricial-precocial intermediate developmental mode; they are mobile shortly after hatching but remain entirely dependent on parental provisioning for their thermal and nutritional needs. This hatchling mass is modest relative to the ultimate adult size, yet it provides sufficient yolk reserves to sustain the chick through its first critical hours. The relatively short incubation period may be an adaptation to reduce exposure to predation and stochastic weather events common in their dynamic coastal nesting habitats.

As the chicks grow under the care of their parents, they undergo a rapid developmental progression fuelled by a diet of small fish and invertebrates. Under the typical active metabolic body temperature of approximately 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the young terns achieve the critical milestone of fledging after a period of 29 days since birth [tx = 29 days since birth]. This fledging age represents the point at which the juvenile attains sufficient flight feather development and neuromuscular coordination for sustained flight, marking its departure from the nest site. The timing is tightly linked to the high metabolic demands of thermoregulation at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], which necessitates frequent feedings by both parents. Field observations indicate that fledglings remain near the colony for several weeks thereafter, gradually refining their foraging skills while still receiving occasional food transfers from their parents before achieving full independence.

The ontogenetic trajectory continues beyond fledging, with juveniles entering a protracted sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and plumage maturation. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal development and the capacity for gamete production, is reached at 87 days since birth [tp = 87 days since birth] when the birds are maintained at an ambient-equivalent body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity in a developmental sense does not, however, translate immediately into breeding activity; first-year birds typically defer reproduction while they refine critical life skills. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Sandwich tern is approximately 250 grams [Wwi = approximately 250 grams], a mass that reflects the species' streamlined, lightly built morphology adapted for efficient aerial foraging over coastal waters. This adult body mass is achieved gradually over the first several months of life as the growing juvenile accumulates flight muscle and fat reserves necessary for migration.

Despite reaching physiological puberty relatively early, the age at first successful reproduction is considerably delayed. The time since birth at first brood for Sandwich terns, under thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolism at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], is approximately 1095 days [tR = approximately 1095 days] — equivalent to roughly three years of age. This prolonged prereproductive period is a common life-history strategy among long-lived seabirds, allowing individuals to accumulate substantial foraging experience, establish pair bonds, and secure a suitable nesting territory within dense, competitive breeding colonies. The delay in first breeding likely contributes to higher initial breeding success and increased lifetime reproductive output. Breeding adults typically lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing one egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing one egg], a conservative reproductive rate that prioritizes chick quality over quantity in an environment where food availability can be unpredictable.

The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, observed in individuals marked as chicks and followed through long-term banding studies, reaches approximately 11242 days [am = approximately 11242 days] under the standard metabolic conditions of approximately 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This remarkable longevity places Thalasseus sandvicensis among the longer-lived of the larid species, a pattern consistent with its relatively low annual reproductive output and deferred maturity. The greatest recorded reproductive rate, expressed as a maximum of one successfully fledged chick per year over a given interval, translates to a mean daily rate that is exceptionally low by avian standards. Such a slow life-history pace — characterized by a long lifespan, delayed first reproduction, and low fecundity — is a classic example of a "slow" life-history strategy. This strategy is thought to be an evolutionary response to the high adult survival rates and the resource unpredictability inherent to pelagic and coastal marine foraging environments.
